intro: 34 instruments, London sessions 2016-10-24 to 2022-12-30 (about 52,000 instrument-days). The chosen walk-forward lines exist only from 2020-08-24 inside this window, so every 'chosen' number is 2020-08 to 2022. 2023 onward is not looked at.

On average the chosen lines are honest: 25.6% of sides go past p75 [24.4, 26.8] against 25%, and 10.4% past p90 against 10%. But not by class: FX majors 27.3% [25.8, 28.9], gold 21.0% [19.0, 23.1], indices 23.5% [22.1, 24.8]. A stop at the p75 line sits too close on majors and too far on gold and indices.

The miss persists. For the plain σ, yesterday's realised-variance miss correlates +0.50 with today's (shuffled: within ±0.02) and is still +0.09 ten days later. The chosen σ, which already feeds back yesterday's and the 5-day miss, halves it to +0.25, but it is not gone.

Feedback still pays on the variance forecast: chosen σ + an error-feedback term has 0.715 [0.666, 0.765] of the plain σ's QLIKE loss, against 0.778 [0.714, 0.831] for the chosen σ alone (2021-22, about 8% better). Even yesterday's realised variance beats the plain σ (0.84). The feedback betas were stable 2018-22 for the plain σ; the chosen ones rest on one year, so treat this as a lead.

On the bands it is much smaller. After a big over-day, 28.3% of sides go past the chosen p75 next day (plain lines 33-34%); after a big under-day 22.4%. Rescaling σ by recent misses cuts band (pinball) loss by 0.7-0.9%; adaptive conformal keeps 25% on average but makes the loss slightly worse (1.002-1.028) and does not fix the quiet-regime miss (29% beyond p75 in quiet regimes, 21-22% in busy ones, for every band built on the plain σ).

Intraday, range used so far is information, not exhaustion. If vol were exactly σ, the most-used tenth at 13:00 would leave 0.80 of the usual range to come and the least-used 1.30. Real days: 1.04 and 1.06, flat, close to the benchmark where today's vol is simply off all day. At 16:00 the most-used tenth leaves 1.25 times the usual.

Drift alarms have something to find: a textbook CUSUM on the plain σ's miss fires about 27 times per 1,000 instrument-days against about 4 on the same misses shuffled in time, every year. For the stop: widen after over-days and narrow after quiet days, by about 3 points of hit rate on the chosen lines; do not shrink a stop because the morning was wide.

charts.title: Daily miss of the chosen forecast: log(range ÷ σ), centred on its own past median
charts.note: 19,311 instrument-days, 2020-08-24 to 2022-12-30 (the chosen lines' honest window). 0 = a typical day for that σ; +0.69 = range twice the typical size. Benchmark: if σ were exactly right every day, the spread of this number from range noise alone would be sd 0.29 (random walk, 1-minute path). Real sd 0.37. For 5-minute realised variance the floor is 0.09 and the real sd 0.45: the RV miss is almost all real forecast error, while about 61% of the variance of the range miss is unavoidable range noise. (The floors assume constant vol through the day and Gaussian steps, so they are a little low.)

charts.title: How often the day goes past the chosen p75 line (OH and OL pooled), by class and instrument
charts.note: Nominal 25% (the reference line). Honest window 2020-08-24 to 2022-12-30. All instruments 25.5866% [24.415, 26.7869] (date-block bootstrap). Classes carry 95% ranges; single instruments do not (about 600 days each, ±3.5 points of noise). Above 25 = lines too tight; below = too wide.

charts.title: Rolling 60-session hit rate of the p75 and p90 lines, all instruments
charts.note: Benchmarks: 25% for p75 and 10% for p90. The plain lines' widths were fitted through 2020-08-20, so before then they are in-sample and should look good. Swings of 10+ points last weeks: misses cluster in time across all instruments (one shock hits many pairs at once).

charts.title: Does yesterday's miss predict today's? Autocorrelation of the daily RV miss
charts.note: Miss = log(RV ÷ calibrated σ²). Benchmark: the same misses shuffled within each instrument, 100 times: 95% of shuffles stay within ±0.022. A slowly decaying positive line means the forecast keeps missing in the same direction for days: a feedback term could still help. The chosen σ already uses yesterday's and the 5-day miss.

charts.title: Loss of each variance forecast ÷ loss of the plain σ (QLIKE, lower is better)
charts.note: 13,451 instrument-days, 400 dates, 2021-01-04 to 2022-12-30 (the chosen σ's feedback term needs a year to fit on). Benchmark = plain σ at 1.0, plus two naive forecasts (yesterday's RV, 22-day mean). Every forecast gets the same past-only scale so only its shape is judged. QLIKE is one of the two losses that rank correctly with a noisy proxy (Patton). Error feedback = σ² × exp(b × yesterday's, 5-day and 22-day misses), b refit each January on earlier years only.

charts.title: Mincer-Zarnowitz slope by year: how much of the forecast's day-to-day move shows up in realised variance
charts.note: log RV regressed on log σ², within each instrument and year. Benchmark 1.0 = the forecast moves exactly as much as realised does. Below 1 = the forecast over-reacts (shrink it toward its average); above 1 = it under-reacts. Plain σ by year; the chosen σ in its window as the last bar.

charts.title: Average miss by year (plain σ): is realised running above or below the past calibration?
charts.note: Benchmark 0 = no drift. The calibration is an expanding past mean, so a year that sits above 0 is a year when realised ran hotter than everything before it. Because log of a mean-one ratio averages below 0 (Jensen), a well-calibrated year sits a little under 0, not at 0.

charts.title: After yesterday's miss: how often today goes past the p75 line
charts.note: Yesterday's RV miss (plain σ) split into fifths per instrument. Benchmark 25% in every row. If a row is above 25 the lines are too tight after that kind of day: a stop placed at the line would be hit more than planned. The chosen lines already scale σ by yesterday's miss, so they should be flatter.

charts.title: Conditional coverage: share of sides beyond the band in quiet, normal and busy σ regimes
charts.note: Plain σ, OH and OL in σ units, 2017-06 to 2022 (each band uses past days only). Benchmarks: 25 for p75 rows, 10 for p90 rows. Regime = where today's σ ranks among its past 250 values. Adaptive conformal fixes the long-run average by construction, so the test is whether it also fixes each regime, and at what width.

charts.title: Quantile (pinball) loss of each band ÷ the static band: judges coverage and width together
charts.note: Below 1 = a better band. Static band = past-only quantile of range ÷ σ, the benchmark. Error-feedback σ = σ scaled by an EWMA (half-life 10 days) of past misses. ACI = Gibbs-Candès adaptive conformal on top of the static band. Same days, same σ, date-block 95% ranges.

charts.title: Overall hit rate of each band (target 25 for p75, 10 for p90)
charts.note: Unconditional coverage only. All four sit near target, which is why coverage alone cannot pick a band: see the regime and pinball charts. Width ratios are in numbers.json.

charts.title: Range still to come after 10:00, 13:00 and 16:00, by how much of the day is used so far
charts.xlabel: surprise so far, decile (1 = least used, 10 = most)
charts.note: Surprise = log(range so far ÷ the instrument's past median range by that hour). y = range added after the checkpoint, ÷ the average at that hour (benchmark 1 = the clock alone). Read the slope: falling = a busy morning leaves less (exhaustion), flat or rising = vol so far carries on. The next chart sets the two random-walk benchmarks beside 13:00.

charts.title: 13:00: real days against two random-walk benchmarks

series.name: random walk, vol exactly σ (every surprise is noise)
random walk, today's vol off by sd 0.23 all day (surprise is information)

charts.note: Both benchmarks use the data's own clock (share of the day's variance done by 10:00/13:00/16:00 = 0.36/0.49/0.78). If σ were exact, a wide morning would leave less to come (geometry: the price is less likely to reach a new extreme). If today's vol is simply higher than σ all day, the curve is flat to rising. Where the real line sits between them says how much of the morning's surprise is information.

charts.title: At 13:00: level of σ against surprise so far. Range still to come
charts.note: Level = σ against its own past-year median (known at the open). Surprise = range so far against the usual by 13:00. Benchmark 1.0. Both measured in σ units, so a pure level effect would already be in σ: a row that rises left to right means level still adds. Slopes per unit (σ units of range to come): surprise -0.0156 [-0.0914, 0.0617], level -0.1097 [-0.527, 0.1404].

charts.title: CUSUM drift alarms on the plain σ's daily miss, per 1,000 instrument-days
charts.note: Textbook CUSUM on the standardised miss (k = 0.5, h = 5, reset after each alarm), each instrument separately. Benchmark: the same misses shuffled in time (50 shuffles), which keeps their size but removes runs. Real alarms well above shuffled = misses come in runs, so a drift alarm has something to find. Years with many 'hot' alarms are when σ lagged a vol rise.

charts.title: Biggest misses of the chosen forecast, 2020-08 to 2022 (6 above, 2 below)
charts.note: Price path from the London open in σ (chosen σ), 10-minute samples. Dashed lines: the chosen p90 lines (OL below, OH above), which a day should cross about 1 time in 10 per side. One per instrument, picked by the size of the miss, not by direction.
